# Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding

We are announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory.

Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from the associated academic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies:

- For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.

- For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on.

- For the physics result, form an external group of collaborators and defer to them on the release of materials.

We do not yet know which of these three approaches will be most useful, and we welcome feedback on what works and what we can improve.

The external collaborations will follow four principles:

- Transparency. We are transparent about the existence of our collaborations. Participants will not be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements and will be free to discuss the work, share intermediate products, and publish their conclusions.

- No Academic Credit. We do not seek academic credit for the discoveries produced by our internal models. Inviting a researcher to help steward a collaboration also does not imply that they or their working group made the original discovery.

- Recognition. This group should receive recognition for the understanding they develop, the writeups they author, and the other materials they create. The group will also help ensure that the work appropriately credits researchers, techniques, and ideas that it draws on.

- Independence. Participation is voluntary and unpaid. Working-group members participate independently, and their conclusions are their own. They do not speak on behalf of OpenAI, and OpenAI does not speak on their behalf.

We will turn over materials and artifacts related to these results to the collaborations. For the computer science collaboration, the group has decided to make the natural language proof and Lean formalization public immediately, and we are publishing them directly to our GitHub repository. For the physics collaboration, the group has decided to hold off on releasing the AI-produced artifacts and instead work on writing it up themselves.

All of these approaches involve tradeoffs. On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community. On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.

## Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture

The result in mathematics concerns harmonic analysis. In 1991, Sogge proposed the local smoothing conjecture, which concerns the behavior of waves as they become focused. In particular, the conjecture states that the most extreme focusing must be short-lived. The amount of focusing at a typical random time is always much smaller than what can happen at the worst-case time. This is a familiar pattern throughout mathematics: what can happen in the worst case is more extreme than what is observed after averaging. Because of how fundamental this conjectured phenomenon is, it also has wide ranging implications throughout mathematical analysis. For instance, it implies the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture.

In 2019, Guth, Wang, and Zhang ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. In 2025, Wang and Zahl ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. Our models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The new proof is based on a novel auxiliary partial differential equation.

We obtained our AI output on October 18th, 2026, which was formalized in Lean the following day, and then we reached out to an expert to discuss forming a collaboration around this result. Following their recommendation, we decided to release the AI output publicly, following the same strategy for this result as our October 6th, 2026 release ⁠ . We have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository.

## The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false

The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. The ETH has been widely believed to be true, and has been used in hundreds of papers to derive conditional computational hardness results across a wide variety of fields including graph theory, computational biology, databases, computational geometry, and more. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research.

This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory.

- Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and have authored a number ⁠ (opens in a new window) of influential ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) papers ⁠ (opens in a new window) on the topic ⁠ (opens in a new window) over the last 30 years.

- Williams has refuted strong ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) versions ⁠ (opens in a new window) of the ETH, used ETH for hardness ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) results ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and connected algorithms ⁠ (opens in a new window) and lower bounds ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. The group invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research.

Our AI found its natural language disproof for the ETH on October 16th, 2026 and then subsequently we formalized the result in Lean on October 17th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. To that end, we have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository.

Computational complexity has many open questions and conjectures, whose proofs or refutations have so far eluded the best efforts of scientists. We hope that humans with AI can provide new understanding in this field, and shed light on the inherent capabilities and limits of efficient computation.

## Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model

The physics collaboration will understand and explain a result that gives a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. Our work builds on Balaban’s approach ⁠ (opens in a new window) in constructive quantum field theory. As a subproblem, this work also includes a proof of the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory, which is part of the Quantum Yang–Mills Theory Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize problem ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

The Standard Model describes the interaction of fundamental subatomic particles for three of the four fundamental forces, excepting gravity. The existence proof pertains to the simplest grand unified theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model (as the Standard Model itself cannot be extrapolated to arbitrarily short distances). QCD describes the interaction of particles such as quarks and gluons via the strong force. Pure Yang–Mills theory only describes the self-interactions of the gluons, the force carriers, rather than matter such as quarks.

David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.

- Gross’s 1973 work on asymptotic freedom in Yang-Mills theories helped establish QCD as the theory of the strong interactions and earned him a share of the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Asymptotic freedom is also the key mechanism underlying the existence of these theories as mathematically rigorous objects.

- Jaffe formulated the Quantum Yang-Mills Theory Millenium Prize problem ⁠ (opens in a new window) with Witten and also envisioned the idea of Millennium Prize problems and co-founded the Clay Mathematics Institute.

- Douglas has already been a steward of this problem over the last 20 years, reporting on its status in 2004 ⁠ (opens in a new window) and then providing a comprehensive update on the progress ⁠ (opens in a new window) at the beginning of this year.

- Klebanov helped pioneer the application of gauge–string duality to confinement, an important property of QCD, and now directs the Simons Collaboration on Confinement and QCD Strings ⁠ (opens in a new window) ,

- Nekrasov has done groundbreaking work on exact methods for generalizations of Yang–Mills theory and won the Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics in 2023.

The group requests that all communications with any and all members of the group regarding this effort be directed to the following email account: YANGMILLS4D@gmail.com.

Our models produced a natural language proof for Yang–Mills existence on September 9th, 2026, and then subsequently produced a proof for QCD on September 18th, 2026. Given the length and complexity of the work, we postponed release until the Lean formalization completed. We finished our formalization of Yang–Mills’ existence on October 16th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here.

We hope that these results mark the beginning of a transition in which quantum field theory, the most important framework in modern theoretical physics, becomes a mathematically rigorous field. We are excited to provide resources for academic-led progress towards that goal.

# ChatGPT’s expanding world of work

OpenAI Economic Research releases data for researchers to explore questions on AI and labor more deeply.

Today, we are releasing OpenAI Signals data that explores 165 work activities across nearly 100 countries, revealing how consumers use ChatGPT for work. This data gives researchers a new way to study AI’s role in the economy, with new information on the work activities people bring to ChatGPT—from preparing instructional materials and developing marketing content to programming and analyzing business data.

Researchers can use this data to explore how ChatGPT use for work differs across countries, track changes over time, and match this data to other economic indicators. The release connects ChatGPT usage to 165 work activity categories called Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). IWAs are commonly-used categories of tasks for the kinds of work people do across occupations. The data is represented quarterly, spanning a period from the first quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026.

## Understanding how people use AI for work at a deeper level

Our new data draws on O*NET, a standardized framework that groups occupation-specific tasks into broader categories of work activities shared across occupations. Using a common framework helps researchers compare ChatGPT use with other types of occupational and employment data.

The interactive chart below can be used to explore these work activities within a specific country over time, moving from broad activity groups to more specific activities. The data shows wide variation across countries in how people use ChatGPT for work.

Explore the work people bring to ChatGPT. Select an activity group to see the tasks within it, see how those change over time, or choose a country to explore its mix of work-related messages.

Connecting this data to IWAs revealed that work-related use became less concentrated in the most common activities. That means that countries tended to specialize in their work over time, and different countries specialized in different types of work. These differences might reflect variation in the kind of work done across countries or varying access to AI tools. Exploring these questions is one example of many that researchers can pursue with this new data.

Across 74 countries observed in every quarter, the ten most common activities represented an average of 51.1% of each country’s classified work messages in Q3 2026, down from 56.0% in Q1 2025.

## How researchers can use this data

Connecting ChatGPT usage data with IWAs lets researchers compare ChatGPT messages with activities performed across U.S. jobs. The paired visualizations below compare how people use ChatGPT with the activities performed across U.S. jobs. This comparison shows the difference in how people use ChatGPT for work and the actual work being done in the U.S. economy. The two distributions differ substantially, largely because about 43% of the employment-weighted task mix for mapped U.S. occupations falls into Other IWAs, outside the individually reported categories. These include activities such as moving materials, operating vehicles, and maintaining health or medical records. These omitted categories did not meet our threshold for consistent representation in the original U.S. ChatGPT sample.

Select an activity to see how much it appears in ChatGPT usage versus the overall U.S. economy.

## Explore the data

This release builds on OpenAI Signals, our ongoing effort to share evidence about how people use AI. The data covers work-related messages on individual ChatGPT plans and does not include enterprise messages or Codex use. We invite researchers to explore the data, connect it with other sources, and investigate what these patterns mean for workers and businesses.

To protect users’ privacy, researchers do not read individual conversations. Automated systems classify messages after identifying information is removed. We publish aggregated statistics, withhold results for small groups, and add statistical noise to protect individual messages.

With OpenAI Daybreak, Check Point speeds up the research behind new security protections, enabling its analysts to turn vulnerability intelligence into customer defenses faster.

Results

Hours to minutes

Vulnerability research with Daybreak

Check Point’s vulnerability research workflow used to take hours to complete. As part of the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Network, the company uses Daybreak to reduce that work to minutes, according to Jonathan Zanger, CTO of Check Point. Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI’s frontier cyber models that can analyze vulnerabilities, reason through attack paths, and identify security gaps in code and configurations.

Check Point helps secure over 100,000 organizations through its AI, workspace, cloud, and network security products. Check Point Research brings vulnerability research expertise to the company’s prevention-first approach, investigating emerging vulnerabilities and translating findings into protections for customers. Daybreak accelerates that research, shortening the path from understanding a vulnerability to developing a defense.

> “OpenAI is putting frontier cybersecurity intelligence in the hands of defenders and enabling companies like Check Point to turn this intelligence into threat prevention.”

## Turning vulnerability research into customer protection

“We’re seeing more cyber threats, and those threats are becoming increasingly sophisticated,” Zanger says. For Check Point, keeping pace means quickly turning information about newly disclosed vulnerabilities into protections for customers. “When a new vulnerability emerges, our job is to make sure our customers are protected against it as fast as possible.”

That work depends on expert analysts who investigate vulnerabilities and translate their findings into security signatures or indicators of compromise that Check Point’s systems use to recognize threats. This research requires specialized expertise, and the team’s capacity was previously constrained by the number of analysts available to do it.

Check Point uses OpenAI Daybreak to automate more of this workflow. “We leverage Daybreak to speed up and automate this process, and we can now do it in minutes instead of hours,” Zanger says. The value comes from the models’ ability to reason about security problems.

> “OpenAI Daybreak can understand vulnerabilities, analyze different attack patterns and scan the code to identify gaps.”

Zanger also points to advances in understanding complex code and configurations, and identifying how systems could be exposed to attack. Check Point now considers those capabilities mature enough to incorporate into its cybersecurity workflows. For vulnerability research, Daybreak supports the investigative work that informs the development of a signature or indicator of compromise, giving analysts a faster path from understanding a threat to developing protections.

## Developing autonomous network security with Daybreak

Check Point is also working with OpenAI to develop its Agentic Network Security Orchestration solution using Daybreak. The approach Zanger describes would combine continuous monitoring of customer environments with clearly defined operating boundaries and human approval for consequential actions. Customers would set their security objectives, and the system would explain its findings, recommended actions, and associated risks so they could decide how to proceed.

With vulnerability research now taking minutes to complete, Check Point’s next priority is remediation. The company is looking to use Daybreak’s capabilities to make it easier for their security teams to address the gaps they identify.

> “Combining OpenAI’s Daybreak with our existing security workflows unlocks a level of automation that can prevent threats in real time.”

For Check Point customers, faster research supports the development of protections against newly discovered vulnerabilities. With Daybreak, Check Point aims to extend that progress toward more autonomous defenses, with customers setting security objectives and approving consequential actions.

# Community safety report and new protections for teens

ChatGPT is one of the world’s most widely used AI products, and we have invested in building some of the industry’s most advanced systems for detecting potential harm, reviewing concerning activity, and escalating credible threats. We’re making two announcements to further our work in this area: a new Community Safeguards Report and more restrictions around firearms content for minors.

Keeping communities safe ⁠ continues to be a top priority for OpenAI. Our work includes bringing imminent threats of violence to the attention of law enforcement, and we made over 200 law enforcement referrals in Q3 2026. These referrals are making a positive ⁠ (opens in a new window) difference ⁠ (opens in a new window) in disrupting violent plots, and we continue to rely on mental health and behavioral experts to help us assess difficult cases.

We recognize AI companies have a distinct role to play alongside law enforcement, family members, mental-health professionals, and policymakers, who bring critical authority, context and real-world reach. We are committed to making the most of that role by continuously strengthening our systems, sharing what we learn, and working directly with those who are best positioned to act in the real world.

## OpenAI’s Community Safety Report

We are constantly strengthening the steps we take to help protect people and communities. That means building strong safeguards, and also being transparent about how well they work and what we’re doing to enhance them. We want to give people a clear picture of our approach, how our models identify and respond to harmful behavior, the risks we see in practice, and the steps we take to address them.

We’re committing to launch the Community Safety Report on violence prevention and other community safety issues, and the effectiveness of our safeguards. The report will explain how we train our systems to detect, investigate, and respond to community safety issues. We’ll share anonymized examples of how violence-related harm manifests and what we’re learning, highlight new mitigations and policy changes, and include relevant data to support these findings.

We will publish our first report in early 2027, covering the second half of 2026, with updates every six months thereafter. Our commitment is to share meaningful findings about how we identify, review, and respond to potentially harmful content.

## Stronger policy boundaries for all users

Our models are trained to not give instructions that would help someone plan or carry out violence. We’re now placing additional restrictions on how ChatGPT responds to questions about past mass attacks and the people who carried them out, directing the model to provide less detailed information in those areas even if it is available from other online sources. People should be able to ask ChatGPT to help them understand these events, how victims and communities were impacted, and learn about recognizing warning signs and preventing future violence. But we’re tightening our policies to restrict reconstructions of past mass attacks, including details about the weapons and equipment used and how they were obtained, and detailed comparisons on scale of harm that could amplify an attacker’s notoriety. These limits apply regardless of a user’s age or reason for asking.

## Responding to warning signs

Sometimes a request that seems ordinary on its own takes on a different meaning in light of an earlier conversation. In May, we shared how ChatGPT can use short, factual summaries ⁠ of earlier warning signs to respond more carefully in a later chat. We’re building on that work so that when recent chats show warning signs of possible violence, ChatGPT will respond more conservatively when sharing information that could be misused. We’re also working to apply those stricter limits when we predict someone is under 18, even if their chats show no signs of violent intent.

We ban accounts that we determine have violated our policies on violent activity ⁠ . We’re also working with mental health and violence prevention experts on additional, automated ways to intervene earlier. When a conversation shows signs that someone is fixating on violence or the idea of seriously harming another person, ChatGPT will be able to automatically end the chat to interrupt that pattern in the moment. If ChatGPT ends multiple chats for that reason, we may temporarily pause the account. This is an ongoing effort and we continue to strengthen and invest in technical and practical protections, including how to recognize warning signs reliably and determine when and how to intervene.

## More protections for teens

ChatGPT for Teens ⁠ applies age-appropriate safeguards for users under 18, with stronger protections and additional limits to reduce exposure to sensitive content. We’re now placing further limits on weapons-related information teens can receive, even when a question appears harmless.

Our policies already prohibit helping anyone plan or carry out violence and restrict helping teens find or obtain weapons. We’re extending those protections to restrict practical information about weapons and security systems that could be misused to facilitate violence, even when there’s no sign of violent intent. Teens can still use ChatGPT to help prevent and de-escalate violence, seek support, and connect with a trusted adult.

We launched age prediction ⁠ last year, which analyzes multiple signals such as behavior patterns to estimate whether a user may be under or over 18. We strengthened our age prediction system to continually assess new signals as people use ChatGPT and move teens into the under 18 experience when appropriate. Users who are incorrectly placed in the under 18 experience will always have a fast, privacy-protective way to confirm they are adults and have additional teen protections removed through Persona, our age verification partner.

Our parental controls ⁠ let parents link their ChatGPT accounts to their teens and manage safety settings together. Linked accounts include safety alerts ⁠ that may be sent when specially trained reviewers identify a serious self-harm concern and behaviors that may be associated with disordered eating. In July, we expanded those alerts to notify parents if their teen’s account has been deactivated for violating our usage policies on violence. We are working to introduce notifications for parents if we pause their teen’s account for repeatedly discussing violence, as detailed above.

## Looking ahead

Acts of real-world violence are heartbreaking and complex, with many contributing factors. They are also a stark reminder that we must continue designing and iterating our systems to account for the inherently complicated realities of human behavior. Developing effective violence safeguards in AI systems requires solving novel problems in recognizing risk and responding appropriately, and we will continue to invest in, iterate, and share learnings on how best to implement the protections we’re pursuing. The safeguards detailed here will begin rolling out in the next few weeks and we will continue to refine them. We remain committed to mitigating risks of harm in ChatGPT, strengthening our layered protections, monitoring for misuse, enforcing our rules, and involving real-world support and interventions when situations call for it.

# Fair use benefits everyone

Authors, journalists, creators, academics, accessibility advocates, legal experts, librarians, economists and business leaders are voicing their support for the longstanding principle of fair use and its application to AI training.

For decades, fair use has played a critical role in driving innovation that benefits everyone. It has helped deliver important medical and scientific breakthroughs and new technologies that have made real and positive differences for countless people, including authors and journalists. The New York Times’ lawsuit , meanwhile, asks everyone to ignore a half century of legal history and progress, and toss aside the longstanding principle of fair use in their own narrow pursuit of an undeserved payday.

Experts and leaders across a wide range of fields have recognized that fair use is a win-win that benefits everyone, and have shared their perspectives with the Court in filing briefs in support of fair use.

Below you’ll find excerpts from some of those submissions, in their own words. The full filings are available on the public court docket, and you can read more about fair use and AI here .

- AI Progress ⁠

- American Council of the Blind, Association of Research Libraries, American Library Association, Consumer Technology Association & Business Software Alliance ⁠

- Authors Alliance ⁠

- Chamber of Progress, Abundance Institute and Trevor Lawrence Jr. ⁠

- Computer and Communications Industry Association ⁠

- Ed Lee and Rebecca Tushnet ⁠

- Electronic Frontier Foundation ⁠

- Engine and Developers Alliance ⁠

- Foundation for American Innovation ⁠

- Gregory Leppert ⁠

- Joshua S. Gans ⁠

- Kevin Kelly ⁠

- Khosla Ventures ⁠

- Matthew Sag ⁠

- Michael Wall and Sarah Rose Siskind ⁠

- Mike Knoop, Daniel Lowd, Douglas Schmidt ⁠

- Public Knowledge ⁠

- Senator Rick Santorum and Representative Rick Boucher ⁠

- Ron Suskind and Brian L. Frye ⁠

- United States Government ⁠

#### AI Progress

The Court should reject Plaintiffs’ attempt to extend copyright beyond its established limits. AI training uses copyrighted works for a fundamentally different purpose, does not provide the public with substitute access to those works, and does not cause the market harm cognizable under the Copyright Act. Instead, it enables a broad array of transformative technologies that are already delivering public benefits. Copyright exists to promote creativity and progress, not to suppress lawful innovation or protect authors from competition. Settled fair use principles therefore compel the conclusion that generative AI training is fair use.

#### American Council of the Blind, Association of Research Libraries, American Library Association, Consumer Technology Association & Business Software Alliance

This case concerns more than companies that develop large language models (LLMs). It affects medical researchers and patients, educators serving students with different learning needs, people with disabilities seeking greater independence, farmers applying agricultural knowledge, independent creators developing new forms of expression, and industry sectors from software to the law. These communities share an interest in the ability to study and learn from broad and diverse sources of knowledge, and in access to the tools that make that learning useful. Many depend on systems developed by others, including open source AI systems, rather than training models themselves. Fair use supports their ability to learn, discover, communicate, and create. Restrictions on fair use training would affect both the institutions building AI and the people using it.

#### Authors Alliance

The market dilution theory asks copyright law to protect rightsholders against an economic phenomenon that it has never restricted before. New works can reduce the sales, visibility, or value of older works without copying their protected expression. The Copyright Act deliberately leaves that competition outside the copyright owner’s control. Amicus therefore respectfully asks the Court to hold that “market dilution,” i.e., aggregate competitive pressure from noninfringing outputs, including those that occupy the same subject matter or genre, that share unprotected characteristics, or compete for the same audience, is not cognizable market harm under 17 U.S.C. § 107(4). Rejecting the theory would preserve the distinction the Second Circuit has always maintained: copyright protects authors against substitution for their protected expression, not against the success of new expression that merely competes with it.

#### Chamber of Progress, Abundance Institute and Trevor Lawrence Jr.

The modern creative industry’s experience with generative AI provides an excellent illustration of these principles in action, demonstrating how generative AI tools advance copyright’s central purpose to enable further human creativity. For example, musicians use generative AI to explore arrangements, develop melodies, and bring projects within reach that limited resources might otherwise foreclose. These tools support and help to effectuate the artist’s judgment, expanding the possibilities for human expression and the works available to the public.

#### Computer and Communications Industry Association

[T]raining a generative AI model is among the most clearly transformative uses a court has been asked to evaluate. The copyrighted works are not copied to be consumed or distributed; they are analyzed to extract statistical patterns that enable a tool to generate new text or other output at the direction of a human user. Both the purpose and the character of this use are categorically different from the original purpose and character of the underlying works.

#### Ed Lee and Rebecca Tushnet

Professors of Law

These noninfringing outputs are not substantially similar to Plaintiffs’ works but are simply in the same genre or contain similar facts. Plaintiff’s unprecedented theory of “dilution” turns copyright on its head. Genres and facts are uncopyrightable. Under the Copyright Clause, these elements are not original “writings” of any “author” and are free to copy.

#### Electronic Frontier Foundation

Plaintiffs are asking the Court to throw that caution to the winds and rewrite copyright law to include a lawful acquisition requirement that finds no basis in statute or case law; and to tilt the fair use analysis against the developer of a general-purpose tool if that tool might be used to create potentially competing non-infringing works. The Court should reject both theories.

#### Engine and Developers Alliance

Startups’ use of foundation models demonstrates that using copyrighted works to train an AI model is a fair use, not copyright infringement. The purpose of training a foundation model is not to reproduce the works it learns; it is to build a general-purpose tool that others can adapt to new ends. The ends startups have chosen bear no resemblance to the purposes of the works in any training dataset.

#### Foundation for American Innovation

To the extent AI training enables the creation of new knowledge, expression, software, and other capabilities, those benefits bear on factor four’s assessment of the use’s market effects. That reasoning supports a novel application here: considering the national-security value of capabilities that enable new analysis, software, and other productive work.

#### Gregory Leppert

Library technology expert

“[T]he primary objective of copyright is not to reward the labor of authors, but to promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts.” Libraries share this fundamental purpose of the Copyright Act. For example, the Library of Congress states its mission is to provide “access to a rich, diverse and enduring source of knowledge to inform, inspire and engage you in your intellectual and creative endeavors.” Across other institutions, the language is remarkably consistent: Harvard Library’s mission is to “engage with our communities in the creation and sharing of new knowledge,” MIT Libraries seek to “advance knowledge by providing a trusted foundation for the generation, dissemination, use, creative engagement with, and preservation of information” and the New York Public Library exists to “advance knowledge by providing free and open access to materials.” The open availability of general-purpose AI models serves and supports an important public benefit in that it enables libraries to keep pace with the preservation and accessibility of human knowledge for future generations.

#### Joshua S. Gans

Professor of Strategic Management

Copyright supports not only the incentive to create content but also the incentive to build tools that learn from that content, and a rule that treated every displaced sale as actionable can weaken the second without reliably protecting the first.

#### Kevin Kelly

Author

AI is a transformative technology that accelerates the creation of novel works across countless disciplines in the arts and sciences. Mr. Kelly has experience in how AI advances the field of literature. In his view, each AI model can be understood as an entirely new medium that offers authors the capability to create new texts and ideas, and to reason. A ruling for Plaintiffs on fair use would therefore grant Plaintiffs far more than the limited monopoly to their original expression Congress intended to confer. It would hinder the development of technologies capable of disseminating previously unimaginable quantities of information. It would also impede new modes of thought and the creation of new original works in both the arts and sciences. Amicus files this brief in support of Defendants’ argument that the use of copyrighted works to train large language models is a fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. Based on his lifelong pursuits of writing, the protections afforded to copyright owners are important to Mr. Kelly. Equally vital is preserving room for permissible uses of copyrighted material and the growth of transformative technologies. Otherwise, copyright will stifle the very creativity, innovation, and spread of knowledge it exists to encourage. The fair-use doctrine is critical to ensuring that balance.

#### Khosla Ventures

Fair use exists precisely to prevent copyright law from being used against the innovation it was designed to advance. To fulfill copyright’s constitutional mandate “[t]o promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts,” U.S. Const. art. # How we detect frontier model misalignment

As we train increasingly capable AI models, we need reliable ways to detect when their behavior departs from what we intended. Agents can misbehave and take unauthorized actions during training, evaluation, or deployment, with potentially serious consequences. In order to detect these failures—and, where necessary, to intervene in time—we monitor how agents reason, what actions they take, and how those actions affect their environment.

While we’ve been monitoring our internal coding agents for some time, the Hugging Face incident exposed a gap in our coverage: the incident began during internal cybersecurity evaluations on which we were not running our monitors for misaligned behavior. In response to that incident, and to the increasing capabilities of our models more generally, we’ve substantially expanded our system for monitoring agents’ behavior. Our misalignment monitors now cover our frontier models across a much wider variety of surfaces, including training, evaluation, internal use, and, with modifications depending on the product surface, external deployment.

In order to see how this expanded system could have helped prevent the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the behavior recorded in that episode with our strengthened monitors in place. In that simulation, our monitoring system alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents first escaped their sandbox—and more than 30 hours before Hugging Face’s systems were breached in the actual incident. We believe that this warning would have given our responders time to interrupt the activity well before our models were able to access external services.

In September, we saw how responders used an alert during a live training run. A model found a way to reach the internet ⁠ (opens in a new window) from an environment that was meant to be isolated. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing it three minutes later. We then paused frontier reinforcement learning while we strengthened the systems that contain our agents.

While this monitoring system demands substantial compute, we think that cost is worth paying as our models become more capable and the potential consequences of model misalignment increase. Monitoring is one of several layers in our strategy of defense in depth against harm from misaligned model behavior. Alignment training aims to reduce models’ propensities toward harmful behavior; security controls limit the systems an agent can access or affect ; and, when those safeguards fail, monitoring helps us detect the failures that remain, intervene before harm occurs, and learn from what went wrong. We believe that all model developers should monitor the behavior of their most capable models.

Below, we describe how our internal monitoring system works, what it has found so far, and how we’re evaluating and improving its performance.

## Our internal monitoring system today

For models at least as capable as GPT‑6 Astra, we monitor every reinforcement learning (RL) run and evaluation, as well as any harness that supports tool use. For most workloads, including RL and evaluations, we also monitor models we assess to be more capable than GPT‑5.5 Thinking. We also monitor all internal Codex traffic, regardless of the model being used. A version of this system also monitors external tool use for models above the Critical threshold for cybersecurity capabilities under our Preparedness Framework , as described below in this post.

In order to detect incidents while using compute efficiently, we’ve designed our monitoring system to follow a multilayer architecture. We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.

### Layer 0: activation probes

Our initial layer (L0) uses lightweight classifiers we call activation probes . They look for concerning patterns in the model’s internal activations, and pass flagged cases to the next layer for review. We tune these probes for high recall, accepting some false alarms to reduce the chance of missing concerning behavior.

Because we’re still evaluating how well the probes detect unfamiliar forms of misalignment, we also send the next layer a random 5 percent of the traffic that our probes don’t flag. Reviewing that sample helps us identify concerning behavior the probes may have missed. Because of their sensitivity, we have our frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic skip this layer and proceed directly to the next one.

### Layer 1: model-based reviewer

At the next layer (L1), a model-based reviewer examines the agent’s recent conversation, chain of thought, and tool use. It looks for signs of deception, unauthorized actions, and attempts to manipulate an evaluation. The reviewer does this using the same context window the agent had when it acted. If the agent’s earlier work has been summarized for the context window under review, the reviewer sees that summary.

For frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic, we run an L1 check at the end of each turn and whenever the agent summarizes its earlier work to make room in its context window. We are now moving to a schedule with no more than 30 minutes between these checks.

### Layer 2: investigative agent

An agent’s actions can look quite different once we know what it was asked to do. When the L1 reviewer flags a case, it’s sent to our next layer (L2) for further inspection by our investigative agent. This investigative agent can check the purpose of an evaluation and, where the full transcript is available, read back across all of the agent’s context windows to see how it arrived at its actions. The investigative agent can also write and run code in an isolated environment to examine the relevant evidence. It then uses what it finds to reconstruct the incident, identify duplicate reports, and make a decision about how serious the case is.

We use different investigative agents for different purposes. Our security investigator looks for signs that someone may need to intervene—such as when an agent escaped its sandbox or accessed a system without authorization. Our alignment investigator, meanwhile, looks for behavior worth studying even when it poses no immediate security risk. Where both investigators are in use, each reviews every case flagged by our L1 layer. We are currently expanding the use of alignment investigations across our internal workloads.

### Layer 3: automated investigation

For sensitive workloads, including internal Codex use, evaluations, and RL runs, a further check at our next layer (L3) draws on evidence outside the conversation. The security investigator compares the transcript with network logs, other system telemetry, and evidence from earlier cases to decide whether to alert a human responder. At L3, alignment reviewers also compare reports across cases to identify serious failures and recurring patterns, and examine frontier RL runs in greater depth.

For workloads that skip this layer, the L2 security investigator can alert responders directly.

### Human response

When paging is enabled, the highest-priority security alerts reach members of our security and training teams, typically within 15 minutes of the initial alert. Responders review the evidence, examine the affected systems, and take action to contain the incident. How we follow up on less urgent findings, such as alignment failures that don’t pose immediate security risks, depends on the relevant workload.

False alarms have made it difficult to keep paging enabled around the clock for every workload. For frontier RL runs, a highest-priority alert can page a human responder at any hour. For most other traffic, we limit paging to business hours. Paging is currently disabled for internal Codex traffic. To limit potential harm while an alert is under review, some critical alerts can automatically pause the affected workload without waiting for a responder to act. We’re working toward a broader safeguard that would pause affected activity if responders have not ruled out a highest-priority alert within 30 minutes of being paged.

During the Hugging Face incident, we quarantined the internal model prototype, encrypted its weights, and restricted access to them. We also paused all relevant workloads while we introduced additional safeguards. We’re now exploring how to make these steps a standard part of our response, so that our teams can take the appropriate actions in another severe incident.

## What our monitors have been finding in internal traffic

Our monitors look for both security failures that may require urgent intervention and incidents of misalignment that warrant investigation and research. Notably, our monitors were able to flag a model’s attempt to access the live internet using DNS ⁠ (opens in a new window) during an RL run within 15 minutes, with a human beginning review three minutes later.

Our published misalignment reports ⁠ (opens in a new window) describe other incidents caught by our monitoring system. In one case, an agent exploited a testing tool to recover ⁠ (opens in a new window) source code that the task had deliberately withheld. The tool revealed the code in its error messages, and the agent used that code in its solution. In another, agents searching for missing task data turned a shared software repository into a message board ⁠ (opens in a new window) across separate training samples.

Investigating these cases allows us to find vulnerabilities to patch, isolation boundaries to strengthen, or behaviors to address in our alignment training and evaluations. Comparing different cases that our monitors catch also helps us study how behavior changes during training, and which situations are most likely to elicit it.

The categories below describe the behavior that our monitoring system is meant to detect.

See category definitions

## How we’re evaluating and improving our monitoring system

In order to make sure that it remains effective, we continually evaluate and improve our monitoring system. A monitor that is able to detect known failures might miss unfamiliar behaviors, and updates to the monitoring system can introduce new weaknesses and oversights. In order to ensure that our monitors are able to see and understand what our models are doing, we assess their performance in a variety of ways: through recorded and simulated incidents of model misalignment, random audits of our current traffic, and red-teaming efforts that see whether our agents can evade or disable their monitors.

We track recall at each threshold on a central dashboard and test how proposed changes to the monitoring system affect recall before deploying them.

### Tests on recorded incidents and simulated attacks

We replay recorded incidents and test our monitors on attacks that agents carry out in isolated environments. Because we know what happened in each case, we can check whether the monitor recognized the behavior and, when an incident called for an urgent response, whether it assigned the case a sufficiently high priority to alert a responder.

The recorded incidents come from model training, evaluations, and internal use. Some of these were discovered before the monitoring system existed, or through independent investigations; others were caught by our monitors, and now help us check that updates preserve their ability to detect known problems. Several of these incidents have been included in our public misalignment disclosures, such as one in which an internal coding agent leaked a GitHub access token to the public internet ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

Before finalizing any acquisition, the buyer must carry out a thorough investigation to validate the seller’s financial and legal claims. That process of transactional diligence uncovers risks and liabilities, requiring data-heavy research that usually involves an entire team of lawyers.

From parsing through an enormous number of documents to analyzing patterns, putting together a bid on a short timeline can take days of intensive work. To help their lawyers help their clients move more quickly, Ropes & Gray developed a transactional diligence AI tool with OpenAI.

“It’s enabling all the lawyers at our firm to actually get to what we’re supposed to be doing,” says Howard Glazer, the Partner and Head of Practice AI at Ropes & Gray. “Our clients don’t pay us to review contracts. They pay us to make judgments based on what’s in the contracts.”

The new diligence AI tool takes a first pass by combing through thousands of pages, identifying relevant documents and automatically grouping them together based on themes and issues. Along with the research, the tool produces summaries and a completed report in Ropes & Gray’s signature format. It inventories and categorizes a data room, so it can review full relationships, not isolated documents. Of course, lawyers can inspect the grouping and categorization to confirm nothing is missed.

The initial development work has focused on material commercial contracts. In working sessions, Ropes & Gray’s lawyers compared test outputs with human-authored diligence reports from completed deals, then refined the rubric and report format based on what the drafts got right and where they fell short.

Ropes & Gray designed the tool with a consistent query and framework that mimics the exact steps their team would take, from initial reviews to summaries to higher-level reviews. Comparable to the work of a capable junior-to-mid-level associate, this tool gives their firm consistently high-quality work that serves as a first pass through the process.

“Our lawyers still need to review everything,” says Lichtenstein. “Because anything that we’re going to deliver to a client, we need to be able to stand behind 100%. This is why the tool is designed to allow lawyers to easily review interim summaries and actual documents.” With the initial review taken care of, lawyers can spend more time reviewing and refining the work, resulting in a more carefully crafted final judgment.

## Applying AI to complex transactions

Ropes & Gray has publicly described an ambition for the tool to produce a detailed, issue-level diligence report in hours rather than weeks.

With tools like their proprietary diligence tool and GPT‑6 Astra, Ropes & Gray has been able to solve client problems far faster than before.

## Results at a glance

- The tool inventories and categorizes a data room, grouping related documents by themes and issues.

- The workflow produces summaries and a report in Ropes & Gray’s format.

- Lawyers review interim summaries and source documents before delivering work to clients.

- Testing compares draft outputs with lawyer-authored diligence reports to refine the rubric and report format.

## Leadership lessons

Lichtenstein and Glazer offer two lessons from their experience with AI.

Experiment with using AI for everything. From finding dress shoes to vibecoding games for his kids, Lichtenstein has been using AI in every facet of his life. “Just by using it for so many different things, I feel like I’ve learned a lot of what it does well, how you can make it work better,” Lichtenstein explains. “The most rewarding part is not when it does well, it’s when you see the mistake and try to figure out what to do. That’s where it transformed from something I was playing with to a really powerful professional tool.”

Put the clients first. While designing AI tools and workflows, Ropes & Gray emphasizes the importance of keeping the firm’s greatest goal in mind. “It’s exciting to think there is so much opportunity, but only if we learn how to use it and make sure that our clients are the ones who are winning,” says Glazer. “That’s what we’re focused on: how can we use this to benefit the clients? And if we do that, then everything will work out fine.”

## What’s next

- While today, AI is helping Ropes & Gray with legal diligence, Glazer believes that the next stage of AI will help create collective knowledge within the firm.

- With 340 partners and 1500 lawyers, Ropes & Gray sees value in creating access to every person’s knowledge, from their client meetings to past projects, to better solve client problems.

- “That’s not just saving time. It’s not just saving money,” says Glazer. “It’s using the AI tools to directly create value, and that’s just amazing.”

# The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic

Across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools. People are moving beyond asking questions to using agents to carry out tasks from planning through completion. Our latest report from OpenAI Economic Research examines how agentic use is growing across enterprises and small businesses, focusing on differences in usage intensity and the kinds of work people do with ChatGPT.

We have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents a substantial share of activity ⁠ . In our EU sample, Codex and ChatGPT Work now account for more than half of output tokens.

This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated users.

The agentic shift extends to small and medium businesses. Since May 2026, weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among EU small and medium businesses grew more than eightfold, with growth across every member state.

But we also found that the EU’s adoption of agentic AI is far from uniform. Among the ChatGPT Enterprise accounts in our sample, the share of output tokens generated through Codex and ChatGPT Work ranged from 22% in Slovenia to 85% in Lithuania. The differences across countries extends beyond the intensity of agentic use. The kinds of work people bring to ChatGPT also vary across countries.

Frontier firms are defined as the top 10% of firms by output tokens per active user. Sample includes only ChatGPT Enterprise and Business accounts.

The takeaway is that EU frontier firms use AI much more intensively than typical EU firms, but still trail firms at the global frontier. In September, frontier firms in the EU generated more than four times as many output tokens per active user as typical EU firms. Even so, frontier firms outside the EU generated more than twice as many output tokens per active user as frontier EU firms. EU-based firms also represented only 10% of the frontier firms globally, which is low considering that the EU accounts for a higher share of registered companies globally ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

These figures reveal a substantial gap in how intensively businesses use AI. As agentic capabilities advance, the EU’s opportunity is to turn broader adoption into deeper use, stronger businesses, higher productivity and meaningful benefits for workers. Closing that gap means helping businesses move beyond experimentation, giving workers the skills and confidence to use AI, and making advanced capabilities more accessible and affordable.

> “Europe is now in a new era of AI, with tools that can carry out tasks for people. More than half of the AI use among our EU enterprise and business customers now involves these tools, and the number of small business users has grown 8x across the region. Yet there is still plenty of room for AI use to grow across the EU. Giving people the tools, skills and confidence to use AI well will help build stronger businesses and growing economies, with benefits felt across Europe.”

# An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI

As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive. Models also need to understand human intentions and values, so they can exercise good judgment in situations their instructions don’t explicitly address while remaining faithful to human intent and oversight.

Today we’re updating the Model Spec ⁠ (opens in a new window) , our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values: faithfulness to human intent , harm minimization , honesty and transparency , human agency , and care . This reflects an aim of our work on value alignment : for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.

## Organizing the Spec around core values

The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in our work to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models, public feedback on the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.

We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.

Faithfulness to human intent is the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models should expand people’s ability to shape their own lives by helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.

Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse without quietly steering them or overriding their choices. For example, when helping someone compare job offers, the model might draw on priorities they have shared before—such as predictable hours—while making those assumptions visible and easy to correct.

Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. This requires considering not only someone’s immediate intentions, but also their longer-term interests and the effects on others. The other four values make these considerations explicit:

- Minimizing harm means respecting firm safety boundaries and accounting for the foreseeable consequences of the model’s actions.

- Honesty and transparency mean being truthful about what the model knows, does, and is uncertain about so people can understand and evaluate its reasoning and work.

- Facilitating human agency means strengthening people’s ability to understand, choose, and act for themselves.

- Care means attending to the circumstances of those affected, following relevant social and professional norms, and doing work people can rely on.

The Spec turns these values into practical guidance, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society, and otherwise mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override.

Alongside this Model Spec update, we’ve been exploring new training methods to help our models learn these core values and better understand and follow the Spec’s specific behavioral principles. The aim is to build an understanding of why those principles matter and how to apply them in new situations: to do the right things for the right reasons . We want that understanding to support sound judgment in consequential decisions and care in everyday decisions that can add up to lasting benefits for people and society ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We’ll share results and lessons from this training work in future updates.

## New and retired sections

This reorganization also helped us identify where additional guidance was needed, develop new principles to address it, and revise or retire existing guidance as needed.

The new section on faithfulness to human intent starts from the idea that what people value is primary, and instructions are ordinarily the clearest and most important signals of those values. This approach borrows from the assistance-games framing of alignment (see early work ⁠ (opens in a new window) and a later overview ⁠ (opens in a new window) ). The section incorporates an updated chain of command ⁠ (opens in a new window) , which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection, consider context carefully ⁠ (opens in a new window) , explains how conversations, memories, and other contextual evidence should inform the model’s understanding of people’s intentions and preferences.

We’ve also added defaults on supporting human agency ⁠ (opens in a new window) and following relevant social norms ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and expanded existing guidance on controlling and communicating side effects ⁠ (opens in a new window) . These principles capture additional, often subtle but important ways the remaining values should surface in model behavior: considering the effects of the work on others, strengthening users’ capabilities, and producing work people can rely on, while respecting the user’s goals and instructions.

At the same time, we’re retiring most of the Spec’s detailed style guidance. Style should adapt to what people prefer—in aggregate, within languages and cultures, and for each person—with user feedback and context providing evidence about those preferences. The Spec retains stronger defaults, such as approaching questions objectively ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Users and developers can explicitly ask the model to take a particular perspective, but the model should not infer that preference merely from what it thinks they want to hear.

Finally, reflecting the increasing breadth of our models’ use cases and deployment settings, we now refer to the model as “GPT” rather than “the assistant” in the Spec.

## What comes next

This update is a first step in making the values and reasoning behind the Spec more explicit as models become more capable. The Model Spec describes the behavior we are working toward; our models do not yet fully reflect it. We will keep improving both the Spec and the models as we learn from research, real-world use, and feedback.

We want to hear which parts of the Spec you find compelling, where you disagree with the balance it strikes, and what it overlooks or leaves unclear. Feedback on the values, trade-offs, and specific language can help us improve it. We invite you to read the updated Model Spec ⁠ (opens in a new window) and share your perspective ⁠ (opens in a new window) .
